MIZORAM PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
COMPETITIVE EXAMINATION FOR RECRUITMENT TO THE POST OF
CIRCLE EDUCATION OFFICER UNDER  SCHOOL EDUCATION
DEPARTMENT, GOVERNMENT OF MIZORAM.
(NOVEMBER, 2025)
GENERAL ENGLISH
Time Allowed : 3 hours
FM : 100
PART- A
(34 Marks)
This Section should be answered only on the Answer Sheet provided.
Marks for each question is indicated against it. Attempt all questions.
1. Write a précis of the following passage and provide an appropriate title.
(14)
Reading or the enjoyment of books has always been regarded among the charms of cultured
life and is respected and envied by those who rarely give themselves that privilege. This is easy to
understand when we compare the differences between the life of a man who does no reading and that
of a man who does. The man who has not the habit of reading is imprisoned in his immediate world,
in respect of time and place. His life falls into a set routine; he is limited to contact and conversation
with a few friends and acquaintances, and he sees only what happens in his immediate neighbourhood.
From this prison there is no escape. But the moment he takes up a book, he immediately enters a
different world, and if it is a good book, he is immediately put in touch with one of the best talkers of
the world. This talker leads him on and carries him into a different country or a different age, or
unburdens to him some of his personal regrets, or discusses with him some special line or aspect of
life that the reader knows nothing about. An ancient author puts him in communion with a dead spirit
of long ago, and as he reads along, he begins to imagine what that ancient author looked like and
what type of person he was. Now to be able to live two hours out of twelve in a different world and
take one’s thought off the claims of the immediate present is, of course, a privilege to be envied by
people shut in their bodily prison. But there is more to it than this. The reader is always carried away
into a world of thought and reflection. Even if it is a book about physical events, there is a difference
between seeing such events in person or living through them, and reading about them in books, for
then the events always assume the quality of a spectacle and the reader becomes a detached spectator.
The best reading is therefore that which leads us into this contemplative mood, and not that which is
merely occupied with the report of events.

3. Read the following passage and answer the questions given at the end:
Toward the end of her day in London Mrs. Drover went round to her shut­up house to look for
several things she wanted to take away. Some belonged to herself, some to her family, who were by
now used to their country life. It was late August; it had been a steamy, showery day. At the moment
the trees down the pavement glittered in an escape of humid yellow afternoon sun. Against the next
batch of clouds already piling up ink­dark, broken chimneys and parapets stood out. In her once
familiar street, as in any unused channel, an unfamiliar queerness had silted up; a cat wove itself in and
out of railings, but no human eye watched Mrs. Drover’s return. Shifting some parcels under her arm,
she slowly forced round her latchkey in an unwilling lock, then gave the door, which had warped, a
push with her knee. Dead air came out to meet her as she went in.
The staircase window having been boarded up, no light came down into the hall.
But one door, she could just see, stood ajar, so she went quickly through into the room and
unshuttered the big window in there. Now the prosaic woman, looking about her, was more perplexed
than she knew by everything that she saw, by traces of her long former habit of life—the yellow
smoke stain up the white marble mantelpiece, the ring left by a vase on the top of the escritoire; the
bruise in the wallpaper where, on the door being thrown open widely, the china handle had always hit
the wall. The piano, having gone away to be stored, had left what looked like claw marks on its part
of the parquet. Though not much dust had seeped in, each object wore a film of another kind; and,
the only ventilation being the chimney, the whole drawing room smelled of the cold hearth. Mrs.
Drover put down her parcels on the escritoire and left the room to proceed upstairs; the things she
wanted were in a bedroom chest.
She had been anxious to see how the house was—the part­time caretaker she shared with
some neighbours was away this week on his holiday, known to be not yet back. At the best of times
he did not look in often, and she was never sure that she trusted him. There were some cracks in the
structure, left by the last bombing, on which she was anxious to keep an eye. Not that one could do
anything. A shaft of refracted daylight now lay across the hall. She stopped dead and stared  at the
hall table—on this lay a letter addressed to her.
(i) Why was Mrs. Drover anxious to see how the house was?
(2)
(ii) Why did Mrs. Drover go to her “shut­up house”?
(2)
(iii) Describe how Mrs. Drover enters the house.
(2)
(iv) What are the things Mrs. Dover notices when she enters the house?
(2)
(v) Find words in the passage that has the same meaning as the following:
(2×1=2)
(a) trickled or flowed
(b) gazed or looked

Direction (Question Nos. 1 - 5) : Identify the parts of speech of the underlined words:

(a) Noun
(b) Adjective
(c) Verb
(d) Preposition
2. You must obey your parents.
(a) Adjective
(b) Verb
(c) Adverb
(d) Noun
3. The harvest is almost ripe.
(a) Adverb
(b) Preposition
(c) Adjective
(d) Conjunction
4. The father divided the inheritance among his daughters and sons.
(a) Conjunction
(b) Interjection
(c) Adjective
(d) Preposition
5. You must have some food, for you are hungry and have a long journey ahead.
(a) Conjunction
(b) Adverb
(c) Preposition
(d) Adjective

Direction (Question Nos. 42 - 46) : Choose the correct option as directed in the bracket:
42. The fire was burning in the forest. (Change to Future Perfect Continuous Tense)
(a) The fire had been burning in the forest
(b) The fire will have been burning in the forest
(c) The fire will be burning in the forest
(d) The fire will had been burning in the forest
43 The man spread false rumours about his wife (Change to Past Continuous Tense)
(a) The man was spreading false rumours about his wife
(b) The man is spreading false rumours about his wife
(c) The man had been spreading false rumours about his wife
(d) The man had spread false rumours about his wife

44.. Mrs. Solis refused to help her husband. (Change to Present Indefinite Tense)

(b) Mrs. Solis was refusing to help her husband
(c) Mrs. Solis refuses to help her husband
(d) Mrs. Solis is refusing to help her husband
45. The farmer has reaped his harvest. (Change to Past Perfect Tense)

(b) The farmer reaped his harvest
(c) The farmer had reaped his harvest
(d) The farmer is reaping his harvest
46. Who is knocking at the door? (Change to Future Indefinite Tense)

(b) Who will knock on the door?
(c) Who will have been knocking on the door?
(d) Who will have knocked on the door?
Direction (Question Nos. 47 - 51) : Select the appropriate direct/indirect speech from the options
given:
47 The teacher said, “It has been raining since this morning”
(a) The teacher says that it has been raining since that morning
(b) The teacher said that it had been raining since that morning
(c) The teacher said that it has been raining since this morning
(d) The teacher said that it was raining since that morning
48. Sarah said, “The soldiers were marching towards the castle”
(a) Sarah said that the soldiers were marching towards the castle
(b) Sarah said that the soldiers had marched towards the castle
(c) Sarah said that the soldiers have been marching towards the castle
(d) Sarah said that the soldiers had been marching towards the castle
49. Benjamin said that he did not enjoy the concert.
(a) Benjamin said,” I have not enjoyed the concert”
(b) Benjamin said, “I am not enjoying the concert”
(c) Benjamin said, “I did not enjoy the concert”
(d) Benjamin said, “I had not enjoyed the concert”
50. Siama said to Kimi, “Why are you sketching on the wall?”
(a) Siama asked Kimi why was she sketching on the wall.
(b) Siama asked Kimi why had she been sketching on the wall.
(c) Siama asked Kimi why she is sketching on the wall.
(d) Siama asked Kimi why she was sketching on the wall.
51. He said, “I saw a rabbit here.”
(a) He said that he had been seeing a rabbit there.
(b) He said that he had seen a rabbit there.
(c) He said that he has seen a rabbit here.
(d) He said that he has been seeing a rabbit here.

Direction (Question Nos. 62  -66) : Choose the correct transformation for the following sentences as
directed against each:
62. Everybody is present.
(transform this into a negative sentence)
(a) Everybody is absent.
(b) Everybody is not present.
(c) Nobody is present.
(d) Nobody is absent.
63. No one can deny that she sings well.
(transform this into assertive sentence)
(a) Everybody accepts that she sings well.
(b) Nobody can accept that she sings well.
(c) Can anyone deny that she sings well?
(d) Nobody can deny that she sings well.
64. It was a lovely day.
(transform it into exclamatory sentence)
(a) Is it not a lovely day!
(b) What a lovely day it was!
(c) Ah! Today is a lovely day.
(d) What a lovely day today!
65 It is useless to cry over spilt milk.
(transform it into interrogative sentence)
(a) Is it useful to not cry over spilt milk?
(b) Is it not useless to cry over spilt milk?
(c) Is it useless to cry over spilt milk?
(d) Is it useless to not cry over spilt milk?
66. Isn’t the building red in colour?
(transform this into a negative sentence)
(a) Is the building red in colour?
(b) The building is red in colour.
(c) Is the building not red in colour?
(d) The building is not red in colour.
